name: Sheiko

card.summary: A family of Russian powerlifting programs built on high-frequency, submaximal training of squat, bench and deadlift, used by lifters to build the strength and muscle that shape a stronger-looking physique.

quick.overview:
Sheiko is the name given to the training programs of Russian coach Boris Sheiko, long associated with the Russian national powerlifting team. The programs organise squat, bench press and deadlift work into many sets at moderate percentages of a lifter's maximum, several days a week.

For looks, the connection is the usual one for strength training: more total training and heavier work can build muscle in the legs, back, chest and arms. Lifters use it chiefly to raise powerlifting totals; a larger, denser physique is a by-product they describe.
quick.how: Lifters pick a published Sheiko cycle matched to their level and follow its prescribed weekly sessions of squat, bench and deadlift plus accessories, with volume tapering toward a meet. Descriptions say average intensity is low, about 70 percent across a cycle, and few sets are taken to failure.
quick.risks: A seminar account of the method notes that high-frequency training is demanding. Lifters on forums discuss whether the volume of a given variant is adequate for their lifts.

lead: Sheiko refers to the training approach of Boris Sheiko, a Russian powerlifting coach. His programs are known for training the competition lifts, squat, bench press and deadlift, several times per week at submaximal intensities, with high total repetitions [1].

Powerlifting is a strength sport in which athletes take three maximal attempts on those lifts [3]. People who train this way build strength, and heavy compound lifting is also used in physique building, so lifters who follow Sheiko-style cycles can gain muscle in the legs, back and torso while chasing strength numbers. Forum discussion of the programs usually concerns performance rather than looks [4].

Descriptions of the method highlight technique practice with loads that rarely reach failure. A coach writing about a seminar given by Sheiko reported average intensity near 70 percent across a preparation and competition cycle [1].

chain: Frequent squat, bench and deadlift sessions
More training stimulus and strength over time
More muscle mass in legs, back and chest
angle.text: Sheiko programs are aimed at powerlifting performance. Lifters who follow them train the big compound lifts often, which is the same movement base used for building muscle.

infobox: About 70% of 1RM on average across a cycle, per a seminar account
Several sessions per week; higher for elite lifters

paras: Accounts of Sheiko programs describe a structure in which each cycle begins with higher volume at lower intensity, then volume falls and intensity rises as a competition nears [1]. A coach who attended Sheiko's seminar reported that elite athletes train 4 to 8 times per week in preparation, with the number of sessions dropping from four per week early in the competition phase to three, then two in meet week [1].

The seminar account describes the approach as submaximal training, contrasted with the near-max work many American powerlifters do, with testing on only a few days and lifters not pushed to true maxes [1].

The seminar account says the approach lets lifters rarely miss reps, which builds confidence and allows focus on technique, and that lighter loads reduce soreness and allow more frequent training [1]. The same account says high-frequency training is demanding [1].
Because the programs prescribe frequent sessions, the same account says high-frequency training is demanding and that the reasoning behind long-term planning deserved more explanation [1].

On the T Nation forum, lifters post about running Sheiko cycles [4][5], ask whether a 3-day version for lifters under 80 kg provides enough deadlift work [6], and compare it with other approaches such as Westside Barbell in a discussion thread [7]. One forum post jokes that after Sheiko, seven sets of squats feel like an easy day [4]. A Sheiko-branded coaching app was discussed in 2019 [8].
